articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 Million Stormwater Problem Has No Fix in Sight
articles.dek: Three years after voters approved a stormwater fee, the county has spent $12 million and completed six projects. Meanwhile, the list of failing drainage systems keeps growing.
brief: Escambia County has completed just six of 89 identified stormwater projects since voters approved a dedicated fee in 2023
The county's priority list has grown from 89 to 127 projects as infrastructure assessments reveal additional failing systems
At the current pace, county officials estimate it would take 18 years to address the backlog—assuming no new problems emerge
articles.body:
The intersection of Lillian Highway and Perdido Key Drive floods every time it rains more than two inches. It flooded last Tuesday. It flooded three weeks before that. It will flood again.

Escambia County knows this. The intersection sits at number 23 on the county's stormwater priority list, a document that has grown by 38 projects since voters approved a dedicated stormwater fee in November 2023. That fee was supposed to fix things.

Three years and $12 million later, the county has completed six projects.

"We inherited decades of deferred maintenance," said Marcus Webb, director of Escambia County Public Works, at a commission workshop last month. "The fee gave us a funding mechanism. It didn't give us a time machine."

The Math Doesn't Work

The stormwater fee generates approximately $8.2 million annually. The county's engineering consultants have estimated the total cost to address all 127 identified projects at $47 million—up from the $31 million estimate presented to voters in 2023.

That $47 million figure assumes 2026 construction costs. It does not account for inflation. It does not account for the projects that haven't been identified yet.

County records obtained by The Flightline show the priority list has grown every quarter since the fee took effect. In Q1 2024, there were 89 projects. By Q2 2026, there were 127. The additions aren't new problems. They're old problems the county is only now cataloging.

"Every time we do a comprehensive assessment of a drainage basin, we find more," Webb told commissioners. "We're not creating problems. We're documenting problems that existed before any of us were in these jobs."

At the current spending rate—roughly $4 million per year on construction, with the remainder going to engineering, permitting, and debt service on equipment—the county would need 18 years to complete the current list. That calculation comes from the county's own capital improvement projections, presented to the commission in May.

Eighteen years. Assuming nothing else breaks. Assuming costs don't rise. Assuming the list stops growing.

Six Projects, Three Years

The completed projects tell a story of limited ambition. Four were pipe replacements—aging corrugated metal culverts swapped for reinforced concrete. One was a detention pond expansion in Ferry Pass. One was a drainage ditch rehabilitation near Ensley.

Total construction cost for all six: $4.3 million. The remaining $7.7 million spent since 2024 went to engineering studies, environmental permitting, equipment purchases, and administrative costs.

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh questioned that ratio at the May workshop.

"We're spending almost two dollars on paper for every dollar we put in the ground," Bergosh said. "I understand there's a process. But the people paying this fee expect to see shovels moving dirt."

Webb's response was measured. Engineering and permitting aren't optional, he said. The county can't excavate a drainage canal without an environmental assessment. It can't modify a culvert without hydraulic modeling. It can't touch anything near a wetland without Army Corps approval.

"The federal requirements don't care about our timeline," Webb said.

Where the Water Goes

Escambia County sits on sandy soil that should drain well. In an undeveloped state, it does. Rain soaks into the ground, filters through sand and clay, eventually reaches the aquifer or runs off to Pensacola Bay.

Development changes the equation. Rooftops, parking lots, and roads don't absorb water. They shed it. That water has to go somewhere, and in Escambia County, "somewhere" is often an aging system of ditches, culverts, and pipes built decades ago for a smaller population.

The county's stormwater infrastructure was largely constructed between 1960 and 1990. Metal culverts from that era have a functional lifespan of 30 to 50 years. The math is not complicated.

"We're not dealing with one failure," said Rachel Torres, the county's stormwater engineer. "We're dealing with an entire generation of infrastructure reaching end of life simultaneously."

Torres presented data at the May workshop showing that 67% of the county's inventoried culverts are past their expected service life. Another 22% will reach that threshold within five years.

The presentation included photos. Rusted-out pipe sections. Collapsed culvert ends. A corrugated metal arch under Nine Mile Road that has visibly deformed under the weight of traffic above it.

That arch is number 4 on the priority list. It hasn't been replaced yet.

The Fee and Its Limits

The stormwater fee passed with 58% approval in 2023, following a campaign that emphasized flooding in neighborhoods like Myrtle Grove, Brent, and Brownsville. Supporters pointed to photos of cars submerged to their door handles, living rooms with six inches of standing water.

The fee structure charges residential properties $5.50 per month. Commercial properties pay based on impervious surface area—the amount of roof and pavement that sheds water into the system. A typical strip mall pays several hundred dollars monthly. Big-box retailers pay more.

Revenue has met projections. The county collected $8.1 million in fiscal year 2025 and is on pace for $8.4 million in 2026. The money goes into a dedicated fund that cannot be used for other purposes.

But dedicated funding and adequate funding are different things.

Commissioner Lumon May raised the possibility of a bond issue at the May workshop—borrowing against future fee revenue to accelerate construction. Webb said his department was analyzing the option but cautioned that debt service would reduce annual construction capacity for years.

"You can borrow to build faster now," Webb said. "But you pay for it on the back end. There's no free money."

No commissioners have formally proposed a bond referendum. No public meetings have been scheduled to discuss one.

What Happens Next

The commission will receive an updated priority list in September. Staff expect it to include at least 12 additional projects identified during summer assessments of the Eleven Mile Creek and Bayou Chico watersheds.

The FY 2027 budget, currently in draft form, allocates $4.8 million for stormwater construction—a modest increase from this year. At that rate, the county might complete eight or nine projects next year.

Meanwhile, the intersection of Lillian Highway and Perdido Key Drive will flood the next time it rains. So will the low spot on Fairfield Drive. So will the parking lot of Bellview Elementary, where parents navigate ankle-deep water during afternoon pickup.

These are known problems. They are documented problems. They are problems number 23, 41, and 67 on a list that keeps getting longer.

"We're making progress," Webb told commissioners in May. "It's just not fast enough for anyone, including me."

The next significant rain in the forecast is Thursday.

articles.label: Feature
articles.headline: The Last Fish House on Pensacola Beach
articles.dek: Joe Patti's grandson runs the only commercial fishing operation left on the island. Developers have made four offers this year. He's not selling—yet.
brief: Marco Patti operates the last commercial fishing business on Pensacola Beach, a 1.2-acre property his grandfather bought in 1961
Four development groups have approached Patti this year with offers, the highest reportedly exceeding $8 million for the waterfront parcel
Patti says he'll keep fishing as long as he can crew a boat, but rising insurance costs and catch limits have him worried about the next generation
articles.body:
The ice machine kicks on at 4:15 a.m., same as it has for sixty years. Marco Patti doesn't need an alarm. He's been waking to that mechanical groan since he was eight years old, sleeping on a cot in the back room while his grandfather sorted the night's catch.

Now 52, Patti runs the last commercial fishing operation on Pensacola Beach. The property—a weathered fish house, two concrete docks and 1.2 acres of Santa Rosa Sound frontage—sits wedged between a $4.2 million condominium tower and a boutique hotel under construction. A hand-painted sign out front reads "Patti's Gulf Seafood" in letters that were red once.

"They see waterfront," Patti said, hosing down the concrete floor where his crew had just unloaded 400 pounds of red snapper. "I see my grandfather's hands."

Four offers, one answer

Developers have made four acquisition offers this year, according to Patti and Escambia County property records. The most recent came in May from Emerald Coast Development Partners, a Destin-based firm that has built three condominium projects on Pensacola Beach since 2019.

Patti declined to confirm specific figures but said the highest offer "would set up my kids and their kids." A source familiar with the negotiations, who requested anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter, said the May offer exceeded $8 million.

The Escambia County Property Appraiser currently values the land at $3.1 million. The structures—the fish house, a small office and a storage building—add another $180,000.

Emerald Coast Development Partners did not respond to requests for comment.

"I told them what I tell everybody," Patti said. "I'll sell when I can't crew a boat anymore. Not before."

What the island lost

Pensacola Beach once supported a dozen commercial fishing operations. Patti can name them all: Bonifay's, where the Margaritaville sits now. The Hernandez place, demolished for the parking garage in 2003. Captain Mike's, which became a t-shirt shop, then a smoothie bar, then condos.

The last one besides Patti's—a small operation run by the Russo family—closed in 2018 after Hurricane Michael damaged their dock beyond what insurance would cover.

"The storms don't kill you," Patti said. "The insurance does."

His own premiums have tripled since 2020, from $34,000 annually to just over $100,000. That's for wind and flood coverage on the structures alone. The boats carry separate policies.

The economics of commercial fishing in the Gulf have grown brutal. Federal catch limits on red snapper—implemented to rebuild overfished stocks—mean Patti's operation can only harvest the species during a 62-day season. Fuel costs have risen 40 percent since 2022. Finding crew willing to work the hours for the pay has become its own challenge.

"I'm not getting rich," Patti said. "I'm getting by."

A grandfather's gamble

Giuseppe "Joe" Patti bought the property in 1961 for $12,000, according to county deed records. He had immigrated from Sicily in 1947 and spent fourteen years working other men's boats before saving enough for his own operation.

The fish house he built still stands, though Marco has replaced the roof twice and the floor three times. The original brass bell his grandfather used to signal the end of the workday hangs by the door, green with salt air.

Joe Patti died in 1989. His son—Marco's father—ran the operation until 2008, when a stroke forced his retirement. Marco, who had been crewing since high school and skippering since his mid-twenties, took over.

"My dad told me once that his father almost sold in 1975," Marco said. "Some hotel company offered him what seemed like real money. He turned it down because he didn't know what else he'd do with himself."

Marco's two children—a daughter in nursing school and a son who works in cybersecurity in Atlanta—have shown no interest in the business.

"I don't blame them," he said. "This life breaks your body. And the water's not what it was."

What comes next

The boutique hotel rising next door—a 72-room project by Innisfree Hotels—is scheduled to open in spring 2027. Its marketing materials promise guests "authentic Gulf Coast experiences," including "fresh-caught seafood from local waters."

An Innisfree spokesperson confirmed the company has had "preliminary conversations" with Patti about a potential supply relationship. No agreement has been reached.

Patti said he'd consider it. He already sells to three restaurants on the beach and ships overnight to accounts in Birmingham and Nashville. Adding a hotel wouldn't change much.

What would change things, he said, is if Escambia County moves forward with a proposed update to the Santa Rosa Island Authority's land-use plan. A draft version circulated in March included language that would reclassify several waterfront parcels—including his—from "marine commercial" to "mixed-use tourism."

The reclassification wouldn't force him to sell, but it would increase his property tax assessment and make it easier for a future buyer to develop the site.

"They're not pushing me out," Patti said. "They're just making it expensive to stay."

The Santa Rosa Island Authority board is scheduled to discuss the land-use update at its August 14 meeting.

For now, Patti still wakes to the ice machine. He still crews a 42-foot trawler called the Maria G, named for his grandmother. He still sorts the catch by hand, same as his grandfather taught him.

"Everybody wants to know what I'm going to do," he said, watching the morning light hit the sound. "I'm going to fish. That's what I'm going to do."

The next boat went out at 5:30 a.m. Patti was on it.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola Prepares for 800 New Personnel as Training Command Expands
articles.dek: The Navy's pilot training consolidation will bring families, cars, and housing demand to a base already stretched thin. The city wants to talk infrastructure. The Navy hasn't returned calls.
brief: Naval Air Station Pensacola will receive approximately 800 additional personnel by early 2027 as part of the Navy's pilot training consolidation program
City officials estimate the expansion could add 2,000 residents to the metro area when accounting for families, straining already tight housing and traffic infrastructure
Multiple requests from Pensacola city staff for coordination meetings with base leadership have gone unanswered since April
articles.body:
The parking lot at Sherman Field fills up by 6:45 most mornings now. Instructors double-park near the hangars. Student pilots walk in from overflow lots three hundred yards out, flight bags slung over their shoulders, moving fast in the July heat.

By January, there will be eight hundred more of them.

Naval Air Station Pensacola is set to absorb a significant expansion of the Chief of Naval Air Training command as the Navy consolidates pilot instruction programs from bases in Texas and Mississippi. The move, announced quietly in a Pentagon budget document last fall, represents the largest personnel increase at NAS Pensacola in more than a decade.

Base officials confirmed the expansion in a written statement but declined interview requests. "NAS Pensacola is prepared to support CNATRA's mission requirements," the statement read. "We are working through normal channels to address facilities and infrastructure needs."

Those normal channels apparently don't include the City of Pensacola.

City Hall left waiting

Since April, city staff have made at least four formal requests to meet with base leadership about the expansion's impact on local infrastructure. None have received a response, according to emails obtained through a public records request.

"We're not asking them to solve our problems," said Marcus Webb, Pensacola's director of public works. "We're asking them to tell us what's coming so we can plan for it."

What's coming, by the city's estimates, is significant. The eight hundred uniformed personnel will bring families. Defense Department housing surveys suggest roughly sixty percent of the incoming personnel will be accompanied by dependents. That translates to approximately two thousand new residents in a metro area where rental vacancy rates have hovered below four percent for three years.

The traffic implications are harder to model. NAS Pensacola's main gate on Navy Boulevard already backs up past Barrancas Avenue during morning rush. A secondary gate on Blue Angel Parkway handles overflow but closes unpredictably for security exercises.

Webb's office has requested data on expected vehicle counts, shift schedules, and any planned gate improvements. The base has not provided it.

Housing market already strained

Pensacola's rental market tightened sharply after Hurricane Sally in 2020 and never loosened. The 2024 arrival of two hundred Navy personnel for a cybersecurity training program pushed vacancy rates lower still. Median rents in Escambia County rose eleven percent last year.

On-base housing at NAS Pensacola operates at ninety-three percent capacity, according to the base's most recent community report. The Navy's statement did not address whether additional housing would be constructed before the expansion.

Local property managers are already fielding inquiries. Jennifer Holbrook, who manages four hundred rental units across Pensacola and Gulf Breeze, said she received calls from Navy families in May asking about availability for January move-ins.

"They're telling me they can't get clear answers from the housing office," Holbrook said. "They're being told to find their own place. But there's nothing available under their allowance."

Basic Allowance for Housing rates for Pensacola, which determine what military families can spend on rent, have not kept pace with market increases. A Navy E-5 with dependents receives $1,647 monthly for housing. Median rent for a three-bedroom in Pensacola hit $1,890 in June.

Schools and services

Escambia County School District officials said they have not received formal notification of the expansion from the Navy. Superintendent Timothy Smith said the district learned of the incoming personnel from news reports.

"We've reached out to the base community liaison office," Smith said. "We're hopeful we'll have a conversation soon."

The district's demographer is attempting to model enrollment impacts using Defense Department averages. Preliminary estimates suggest between three hundred and four hundred additional students across elementary, middle, and high school levels. Most would likely enroll in schools west of downtown—Warrington Elementary, Workman Middle, Pensacola High.

Warrington Elementary is already at ninety-one percent capacity.

A familiar pattern

The communication gap between NAS Pensacola and local government is not new. When the Navy announced plans to expand the National Flight Academy in 2019, city officials learned of traffic and utility impacts weeks before construction began. A planned runway extension in 2021 proceeded without coordination on noise abatement, drawing complaints from residents in Warrington and Brownsville.

Council member Delores Henderson, whose District 7 includes neighborhoods adjacent to the base, said the pattern is frustrating but predictable.

"They're a federal installation. They don't have to talk to us," Henderson said. "But we're the ones who answer the phones when constituents can't find housing or can't get to work because the gate's backed up to I-10."

Henderson said she plans to raise the issue at the council's July 22 meeting and request that Mayor D.C. Reeves formally petition the base commander for a coordination meeting.

The mayor's office did not respond to a request for comment.

What comes next

The first wave of personnel transfers is scheduled for October. Full implementation is expected by March 2027.

At Sherman Field last Tuesday, a T-6 Texan II lifted off the runway and banked south over the bay. Then another. Then another. Twelve training flights in forty minutes. A pace that will only increase.

The base's written statement concluded with a single forward-looking line: "We value our partnership with the Pensacola community and look forward to continued collaboration."

Webb, the public works director, read that line aloud when shown the statement.

"Collaboration requires communication," he said. "We're still waiting."
